en.title: Prices and paying
en.summary: Saying prices correctly and paying by cash or card.

paragraphs: Prices are one of the first things to say aloud in a foreign language. This lesson teaches you to read, say and ask about prices and to deal with the checkout.
A customer is paying for a scarf at a shop in Edinburgh.

lines.speaker: Cashier
lines.text: The hat is eight ninety-nine, so both together are twenty-one pounds forty-nine.

lines.speaker: Cashier
lines.text: Yes, of course. You can tap your card here, or insert it and enter your PIN.

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.text: Could I have a receipt, please?

lines.speaker: Cashier
lines.text: Certainly. Here you are. Have a nice day.

paragraphs: **1. Say prices in full.** A price with pounds and pence is said as two numbers; the second number can be said without pence. See Introduction to Grammar: Numerals.

**2. Can I and could I ask politely.** Could is a little more polite than can, and I'd like is polite when you ask for something. See Introduction to Grammar: Moods, command, subjunctive and conditional.

blocks.html:
PhraseExample
Can I...?Can I pay by card?
Could I...?Could I have a receipt, please?
I'd like...I'd like to pay in cash.
Do you take...?Do you take credit cards?

items: Cash, card and contactless are the usual ways of paying.
Change is the money you get back; a receipt shows what you bought.
Price is a noun, and cost can be a noun or a verb: It costs ten pounds.
A discount is a lower price, and VAT is the tax included in many prices in Britain.

paragraphs: Contactless payment is so common in Britain that many small shops and buses no longer take cash. In the United States prices in shops are shown without tax, which is added at the till, so the total is higher than the label.
